questions.q: A chemical equation is balanced to satisfy the law of:
questions.solution:
Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical change, so each element must appear in equal numbers on both sides — the **law of conservation of mass**.

A reaction rearranges the same building blocks; it never adds or removes any.

Two substances join to make one — a **combination** reaction.

It is also strongly **exothermic**: slaking lime releases enough heat to boil the water it is mixed with.

questions.q: In the reaction $\text{CuO} + \text{H}_{2} \to \text{Cu} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$, the substance reduced is:
questions.solution:
**$\text{CuO}$ loses oxygen**, so it is **reduced** (to copper).

$\text{H}_{2}$ gains oxygen, so it is oxidised. Both happen together, which is why such reactions are called **redox**.

questions.q: The black coating that forms on silver articles is:
questions.solution:
Silver reacts with traces of hydrogen sulphide in the air to give black **silver sulphide**.

Copper goes green ($\text{CuCO}_{3}\cdot\text{Cu(OH)}_{2}$) and iron goes brown (hydrated $\text{Fe}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$). Three metals, three different corrosion products.

questions.q: Chips are packed in nitrogen gas to prevent:
questions.solution:
Flushing the packet with **nitrogen** displaces oxygen, so the fats cannot oxidise and turn rancid.

Antioxidants and airtight containers do the same job by other means. Nitrogen is chosen because it is cheap, plentiful and almost completely unreactive.

questions.q: In the balanced equation $a\,\text{Fe} + b\,\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \to \text{Fe}_{3}\text{O}_{4} + c\,\text{H}_{2}$, find the value of $b$.
questions.solution:
Three iron atoms are needed, so $a = 3$.

$\text{Fe}_{3}\text{O}_{4}$ needs four oxygens, and each comes from one water molecule, so $b = \mathbf{4}$ (and then $c = 4$).

Balance the element that appears in the fewest places first — here oxygen.

questions.q: In the balanced equation for the burning of magnesium, $a\,\text{Mg} + \text{O}_{2} \to b\,\text{MgO}$, find the value of $b$.
questions.solution:
$2\text{Mg} + \text{O}_{2} \to 2\text{MgO}$, so $b = \mathbf{2}$.

The oxygen molecule supplies two atoms, so two magnesium atoms are needed to take them.

questions.q: Find the molar mass of calcium carbonate, $\text{CaCO}_{3}$, in g/mol. (Ca $= 40$, C $= 12$, O $= 16$.)
How many atoms in total are present in one formula unit of $\text{Ca(OH)}_{2}$?
questions.solution:
One Ca, two O and two H: $1 + 2 + 2 = \mathbf{5}$.

The subscript outside the bracket multiplies everything inside it.

questions.q: In $\text{Pb(NO}_{3})_{2} \to \text{PbO} + a\,\text{NO}_{2} + b\,\text{O}_{2}$, the balanced equation uses $2\,\text{Pb(NO}_{3})_{2}$. Find $a$.
questions.solution:
$2\text{Pb(NO}_{3})_{2} \to 2\text{PbO} + 4\text{NO}_{2} + \text{O}_{2}$.

Four nitrogen atoms on the left give four $\text{NO}_{2}$: $a = \mathbf{4}$.

This is the reaction that gives the brown fumes when lead nitrate is heated in a test tube.

questions.q: Define and give one balanced example each of a decomposition, a displacement and a double displacement reaction.
questions.solution:
**Decomposition** — one substance breaks into two or more.

$2\text{Pb(NO}_{3})_{2} \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} 2\text{PbO} + 4\text{NO}_{2} + \text{O}_{2}$

Decomposition can be driven by heat, light (silver chloride greying in sunlight) or electricity (electrolysis of water).

**Displacement** — a more reactive element pushes out a less reactive one.

$\text{Fe} + \text{CuSO}_{4} \to \text{FeSO}_{4} + \text{Cu}$

The blue solution fades and a red-brown deposit appears on the iron nail.

**Double displacement** — two compounds exchange partners.

$\text{Na}_{2}\text{SO}_{4} + \text{BaCl}_{2} \to \text{BaSO}_{4}\downarrow + 2\text{NaCl}$

When one product is insoluble it falls out as a **precipitate**, which is what drives the reaction forward.

questions.q: Define oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen and hydrogen, and identify both in $\text{ZnO} + \text{C} \to \text{Zn} + \text{CO}$.
questions.solution:
**Oxidation** — gain of oxygen, or loss of hydrogen.

**Reduction** — loss of oxygen, or gain of hydrogen.

**In the given reaction:**

• $\text{ZnO}$ **loses** oxygen $\to$ **reduced** to Zn.

• $\text{C}$ **gains** oxygen $\to$ **oxidised** to CO.

So carbon is the **reducing agent** and zinc oxide the **oxidising agent**.

The two always happen together — one substance can only lose oxygen if another takes it. That is why the pair is called a **redox** reaction, and why identifying one half tells you the other.

questions.q: What is corrosion? Describe the rusting of iron and three ways to prevent it. Then explain rancidity and how it is prevented.
questions.solution:
**Corrosion** — the gradual eating away of a metal by the attack of air, moisture or chemicals around it.

**Rusting** needs **both air and water**: neither alone will do it, which is why iron does not rust in dry air or in boiled, air-free water.

$4\text{Fe} + 3\text{O}_{2} + x\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \to 2\text{Fe}_{2}\text{O}_{3}\cdot x\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

Rust flakes away instead of sticking, so fresh metal is always exposed and the attack works inwards until the object is destroyed.

**Prevention.**

1. **Painting, oiling or greasing** — keeps air and water off.

2. **Galvanising** — a coat of zinc, which corrodes in the iron's place and protects it even where the coating is scratched.

3. **Alloying** — stainless steel (iron with chromium and nickel) does not rust at all.

**Rancidity** — the oxidation of fats and oils in food, giving an unpleasant smell and taste.

**Prevented by:** adding **antioxidants**; packing in **nitrogen**; refrigeration; and keeping food in airtight containers away from light.

**Step 1 — count both sides.** Left: 1 Fe, 2 H, 1 O. Right: 3 Fe, 2 H, 4 O.

**Step 2 — balance iron.** Put 3 in front of Fe.

$3\text{Fe} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \to \text{Fe}_{3}\text{O}_{4} + \text{H}_{2}$

**Step 3 — balance oxygen.** Four are needed on the left, so put 4 in front of water.

$3\text{Fe} + 4\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \to \text{Fe}_{3}\text{O}_{4} + \text{H}_{2}$

**Step 4 — balance hydrogen.** Eight on the left, so 4 molecules of hydrogen on the right.

$\mathbf{3\text{Fe} + 4\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \to \text{Fe}_{3}\text{O}_{4} + 4\text{H}_{2}}$

**Check:** Fe 3 = 3, H 8 = 8, O 4 = 4. ✓

Never change a formula to balance an equation — only the numbers in front.

questions.q: Distinguish between exothermic and endothermic reactions with one example each, and give one everyday instance of each.
questions.solution:
**Exothermic** — heat is **given out**, so the surroundings warm up.

$\text{CaO} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \to \text{Ca(OH)}_{2} + \text{heat}$

Everyday: **respiration** — glucose is oxidised in our cells, releasing the energy that keeps us warm and moving. Also the burning of any fuel.

**Endothermic** — heat is **absorbed**, so the surroundings cool.

$\text{CaCO}_{3} + \text{heat} \to \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_{2}$

Everyday: **photosynthesis** — plants take in energy from sunlight to build glucose from carbon dioxide and water.

The two examples are worth holding together: respiration and photosynthesis are very nearly one another's reverse, and between them they move energy from the Sun into everything that lives.
